headings.title: Introduction to Dermatological Assessment
headings.content: A comprehensive dermatological assessment is foundational for nursing students in Nigeria to accurately identify, evaluate, and monitor skin disorders in diverse healthcare settings. The assessment begins with a thorough health history, capturing the patient's chief complaint, onset, duration, progression, and associated symptoms of any skin changes. Nurses must also inquire about a personal or family history of skin conditions, allergies, occupational exposures, recent travel, and medications, as these factors frequently precipitate or exacerbate dermatological pathologies. Following the history, a systematic physical examination is conducted. Optimal assessment requires adequate lighting, preferably natural daylight, and full exposure of the skin while maintaining the patient's privacy and dignity. The nurse inspects the entire integumentary system, including the scalp, nails, and mucous membranes, noting the general distribution, configuration, and morphology of any lesions. Palpation is then utilized to assess skin texture, turgor, temperature, and moisture levels, as well as the characteristics of specific lesions such as mobility, tenderness, and depth. Documenting these findings accurately helps establish a baseline, aids the multidisciplinary team in formulating a diagnosis, and evaluates the ongoing effectiveness of prescribed nursing and medical interventions. Recognizing normal variations across different skin tones is especially crucial in the Nigerian context, where melanin-rich skin may present distinct visual cues for conditions like inflammation, cyanosis, or jaundice compared to lighter skin types. Mastering these foundational assessment skills empowers nursing students to deliver holistic, culturally competent care and detect early signs of localized disease or systemic compromise.

headings.title: Primary Skin Lesions
headings.content: Primary skin lesions are the initial, spontaneous manifestations of a pathological process on previously normal skin. Understanding these lesions is essential for accurate clinical identification and documentation by nursing students. Primary lesions are categorized based on their size, elevation, and content. Flat, non-palpable changes in skin color are classified as macules if they are less than one centimeter in diameter, such as freckles or flat moles, whereas patches are larger than one centimeter, like café-au-lait spots. Elevated, solid lesions include papules (less than one centimeter, such as a small elevated mole or wart), plaques (broad, elevated lesions greater than one centimeter often formed by coalescing papules, typical in psoriasis), and nodules (deeper, firm, palpable masses greater than one centimeter). Fluid-filled primary lesions vary by size and the type of fluid they contain. Vesicles are small, fluid-filled blisters less than one centimeter, commonly seen in herpes simplex or varicella, while larger fluid collections are termed bullae, as observed in second-degree burns or pemphigus. Pustules are elevated lesions filled with purulent fluid or pus, characteristic of acne or folliculitis. Wheals represent transient, localized areas of cutaneous edema, such as in urticaria or insect bites, caused by dermal fluid leakage. Recognizing these distinct morphological features allows nurses to communicate findings precisely, support medical diagnoses, and plan targeted nursing care for patients experiencing various dermatological conditions.

headings.title: Secondary Skin Lesions
headings.content: Secondary skin lesions develop from changes to primary lesions over time, or as a result of external trauma, scratching, or the natural evolution and healing of a disease process. Recognizing these lesions helps nurses evaluate disease progression, severity, and potential complications such as secondary bacterial infections. Depressed secondary lesions include erosions, which are moist, circumscribed, shallow losses of the epidermis that heal without scarring, and ulcers, which represent deeper losses of both the epidermis and dermis, typically healing with scar formation, as seen in pressure injuries or venous stasis ulcers. Fissures are linear cracks or breaks in the skin extending into the dermis, often painful and prone to infection, commonly found at the corners of the mouth or between toes. Material accumulation on the skin surface creates other distinct secondary lesions. Crusts, commonly known as scabs, are dried serum, blood, or purulent exudate on the skin surface. Scales are heaped-up, keratinized cells that flake off, characteristic of conditions like psoriasis or exfoliative dermatitis. Lichenification involves a thickening and roughening of the skin with accentuated skin markings, resulting from repeated scratching or rubbing, which is frequently observed in chronic eczema. Scars and keloids represent the replacement of destroyed dermal tissue by fibrous tissue, with keloids extending beyond the original borders of the wound due to excessive collagen formation. A careful assessment of these secondary changes is crucial for preventing further skin damage and promoting effective wound healing.

headings.title: Vascular and Purpuric Lesions
headings.content: Vascular and purpuric lesions involve abnormalities of the blood vessels within the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Understanding these lesions is vital for nursing students because they can indicate local skin trauma, systemic bleeding disorders, vascular malformations, or serious systemic infections. Vascular lesions often result from dilated or newly formed blood vessels. Spider angiomas are central red spots with radiating reddish extensions that blanch with pressure, commonly associated with liver disease or estrogen surges. Telangiectasias are permanently dilated small blood vessels appearing as fine, irregular red lines on the skin surface. Cherry angiomas are small, smooth, cherry-red papules that are benign and increase with normal aging. Purpuric lesions result from extravasation of blood out of the vascular system and into the surrounding skin or mucous membranes. Unlike vascular lesions, purpuric lesions do not blanch (turn white) when pressure is applied, a critical diagnostic hallmark known as diascopy. Petechiae are tiny, pinpoint, non-blanching red or purple spots, measuring less than three millimeters, frequently associated with thrombocytopenia, clotting disorders, or severe infections like meningococcemia. Purpura refers to larger confluent areas of hemorrhage measuring between three millimeters and one centimeter, while ecchymoses, commonly known as bruises, are larger patches of extravasated blood resulting from trauma or bleeding tendencies. Evaluating the color, size, blanching ability, and distribution of these lesions helps nurses identify emergencies and report critical changes promptly to the healthcare team.

headings.title: Subjective Symptoms: Pruritus, Pain, and Sensory Alterations
headings.content: Subjective symptoms accompanying dermatological conditions—primarily pruritus, pain, and sensory alterations—greatly impact a patient's physical comfort and psychological well-being. Pruritus, or itching, is one of the most common and distressing symptoms in dermatology. It can be localized, as in contact dermatitis or insect bites, or generalized, often pointing toward systemic issues like chronic renal failure, cholestatic liver disease, or lymphomas. The itch sensation is transmitted by unmyelinated C-fibers in the epidermis and dermal-epidermal junction, sharing pathways with pain. Scratching provides temporary relief by overriding the itch signal with a pain signal, but it triggers an itch-scratch cycle that leads to secondary lesions like excoriations and lichenification, increasing the risk of secondary bacterial infections. Pain and burning sensations in the skin can stem from inflammatory processes, tissue destruction, or nerve involvement. For example, the sharp, burning pain of shingles (herpes zoster) follows a distinct dermatomal distribution and can persist long after the rash resolves as post-herpetic neuralgia. Sensory alterations such as numbness, tingling (paresthesia), or hyperesthesia may indicate neuropathic involvement, vitamin deficiencies, or localized nerve compression. Nursing students must thoroughly assess these subjective symptoms by evaluating their onset, triggers, severity using a standardized pain or itch scale, and effect on sleep and daily activities, thereby guiding effective comfort and management measures.

headings.title: Systemic Manifestations of Dermatological Conditions
headings.content: Dermatological conditions are rarely isolated to the skin; many serve as external manifestations of complex systemic diseases. Nursing students must recognize that skin changes can reflect endocrine, autoimmune, infectious, or malignant processes occurring internally. For instance, generalized pruritus and xerosis (extreme dry skin) can be early indicators of chronic kidney disease or diabetes mellitus due to metabolic alterations and dehydration of the stratum corneum. Autoimmune disorders frequently present with characteristic cutaneous markers: systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is classic for its malar 'butterfly' rash across the bridge of the nose and cheeks, which worsens with sun exposure. Infectious diseases often manifest with specific exanthems, such as the rash of measles, chickenpox, or the generalized lymphadenopathy and skin manifestations of advanced HIV/AIDS. Furthermore, endocrine disorders like hypothyroidism can cause dry, coarse, cool skin and hair thinning, whereas hyperthyroidism may present with warm, smooth, moist skin and localized myxedema. Nutritional deficiencies also reveal themselves through the skin; pellagra (niacin deficiency) presents with hyperpigmented lesions in sun-exposed areas. Recognizing these systemic manifestations enables nurses to look beyond the surface, collaborate with multidisciplinary healthcare teams, and advocate for comprehensive diagnostic evaluations that address the patient's overall health status.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Documentation of Skin Disorders
headings.content: Accurate nursing assessment and documentation are critical components of professional nursing practice when caring for patients with skin disorders. Documentation must be precise, objective, and comprehensive, utilizing standard medical terminology to describe lesion characteristics. When documenting a skin lesion, nurses should record its exact anatomical location, distribution (localized, generalized, symmetric, or asymmetric), configuration (linear, clustered, annular, or coalescing), and morphology (primary and secondary lesion types). Dimensions—specifically length, width, and depth in centimeters—must be measured using a ruler rather than estimated. Color variations, exudate characteristics (amount, color, and odor), and the presence of surrounding erythema or warmth should also be detailed. Standardized tools like the Braden Scale for pressure injury risk or the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) are frequently utilized to quantify risk and monitor clinical progression over time. In addition to physical findings, nursing documentation must capture the patient's subjective experience, including pain and itch levels, and evaluate the effectiveness of interventions such as topical applications, dressings, or systemic therapies. Clear, serial documentation ensures continuity of care among healthcare shifts, facilitates accurate communication with physicians and wound care specialists, and provides legal protection by establishing a clear timeline of patient assessment and nursing actions.
